author: Brian Hioe
title: May Chin Indictment Gestures Toward Extensive Reach of Chinese United Front Work
content:
INDEPENDENT PAN-BLUE legislator Kao Chin Su Mei, also known as May Chin or Ciwas Ali, and who is an Indigenous legislator of the Atayal people, has been indicted for Chinese United Front work. According to prosecutors, Chin accepted more than 170 million NTD, which was funneled to organizations, relatives, and other bodies in order to conduct influence operations aimed at winning elections. Prosecutors are seeking 14 years for Chin, who was previously facing charges about illegally importing Chinese COVID-19 vaccines for distribution among her constituents.

The networks of these organizations were managed by her office director, Chang Chun-chieh, and legislative assistants Chen Chih-huang and Lin Yi-chun. Chang is currently under investigation for having fled overseas by boat in order to avoid arrest, with authorities conducting raids earlier this month to find the vessel on which he escaped. Chang and Chen reportedly coordinated United Front efforts, while Lin acted as an intermediary with China. Chin has been accused of using her influence as a legislator in order to influence government policy in arms sales, defense, cross-strait relations, and international relations.

For her part, Chin has denied participation in such United Front work, suggesting that she did not need Chinese support to win elections. Chin also raised questions about why she was apparently under surveil

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: “My Body Is My Own”: Collective Memory, Remembrance, and Dignity in Taiwan Transgender and Intersex History
content:
This article submission was originally published by 跨服TransServer’s trans co-created column, Trans Day Reader and is syndicated here on New Bloom Magazine’s website with 跨服TransServer’s permission. In the original article, TransServer writes the following introduction:

November is Transgender Awareness Month and November 8th is Intersex Day of Remembrance. For the author, November 8th carries the weight of intertwined histories of medical violence within transgender and intersex communities, as well as the responsibility of building solidarity across these communities. Choosing this day to begin HRT, Yo-Ling offers this Trans Day Reader as an act of intervention, grounding its significance within the Taiwanese context.

The medical establishment profoundly impacts intersex well-being, as medical authority often overshadows bodily autonomy for intersex people. At the same time, scholars shape collective memory by ghostwriting for historical subjects. Positioned with critique and reflexivity, this article revisits archives of Mr. Xie Jianshun’s gender transition under duress, but more importantly, his acts of resistance, which advance a politics of self-respect for Sinophone trans and intersex communities. In reaching a wider public, readers must recognize academic critique as an autonomous domain and respect the author’s embodied self-disclosure.

NOVEMBER 8TH is both my gender affirming hormone therapy anniversary day, as well as Intersex Day of Remembrance. There is a story and a set of political reasons for choosing this particular date to start hormones. I am a Taiwanese transgender activist, as well as an independent scholar of transgender studies and Taiwanese postwar trans history. The first recorded use of hormones for gender transition in Taiwan is from the 1950s and was far from “gender affirming.” May this Trans Day Reader entry be a reminder to us all that holding our own collective memory is a form of resistance, especially when our histories have been written by scholars profiting off of our suffering, distorting and reproducing the realities of medical and archival violence, and damaging the intertwined dignity of Sinophone trans and intersex peoples.

On August 14, 1953, doctors at No. 518 Hospital of the ROC Army (陸軍第518醫院) in Tainan discovered that a soldier named Xie Jianshun (謝尖順) had intersex characteristics. The doctors performed an exploratory laparotomy on August 20 to determine Xie’s “true biological sex” and decided that he was anatomically “female” due to his having a uterus, two ovaries, and fallopian tubes. Doctors subsequently decided for Xie that he should receive “sex change” procedures, which included further surgeries and feminizing hormone therapy, in order to become a woman. [1] Xie expressed a strong desire to continue living his life as a man, even going so far as to tell reporters on August 21, after undergoing exploratory laparotomy, that he would rather kill himself than become a woman (United Daily News, 1953/08/21). Indeed, throughout the course of medical treatment and afterwards, archival materials surrounding Xie’s gender transition consistently demonstrate Xie’s self-conceptualization as a man and deep discomfort being both misgendered as and medically transitioned into a woman.

When Xie was ordered to be moved from No. 518 Hospital in Tainan to No. 1 General Hospital in Taipei (陸海空軍第一總醫院) later in 1953 to receive further “sex change” procedures, he told reporters that “I have already decided not to go up to Taipei. Whoever wants me to go to Taipei is better off sending me two bullets. I would rather die than comply. Although I am a soldier for whom obedience is my duty, my body is my own. I have the freedom to decide what to do with my own body” (Min Sheng Daily, 1953/12/09). Despite his explicit refusal, he was relocated to Taipei in early 1954 to continue receiving “treatments.”

In the fall of 1955, doctors at No. 1 General Hospital in Taipei decided for Xie that in order for him to “be able to become a mother” and have “menstrual bleeding that is the same as regular women,” and also for the sake of “achieving an even more tremendous advancement in medical research,” they would specially purchase injectable estrogen for Xie (United Daily News, 1955/10/15). Regarding how Xie felt about being injected with estrogen, news reports record him sharing “the pain of having needles inserted into [his] body is only secondary; watching [his] body change day by day is what really causes [him] anxiety” (United Daily News, 1955/10/17). Under the “care” of the military hospital system in 1950s Taiwan as a soldier, Xie could only accept what was being done to his body and practice refusal in line with his understanding of himself as a man in small yet powerful moments—such as in his refusals to wear a qipao during his hospital stay, and his refusal wear women’s clothing and to allow others to refer to him as a woman or to call him “Miss Xie” after finally being discharged from No. 1 General Hospital to live and work at the Ta Tung Relief Institute for Women and Children (大同婦孺教養院) on September 16, 1958 (United Daily News, 1964/12/16).

Before being discharged, Ta Tung’s founding director Madam Huang-Lu Hsiao-chu (黃盧小珠女士) told reporters that Ta Tung was “preparing to assist [Xie] in reconstructing [his] psychology” to be in alignment with his re-assigned sex as a woman (United Daily News, 1958/09/04). While existing historical records do not detail how exactly Ta Tung, as an institution, sought to “reconstruct [Xie’s] psychology,” given the institution’s background as a Christian relief organization, it is reasonable to infer that techniques including talk therapy counseling and “spiritual guidance” sessions aimed at encouraging Xie to live his new life at Ta Tung as a woman. The scarce amount of archival materials we have during Xie’s time at Ta Tung shows that he “rejected ‘spiritual guidance’ from missionaries” (United Daily News, 1964/12/16). While it is unclear what exactly transpired during Xie’s stay at Ta Tung, what is clear is that in the last media report we have of him after over six years of stay, Xie is described as “depressed” and “negative,” “feeling that [his] sex change was a tragic event, and hence resenting the doctors who operated on [him]” (United Daily News, 1964/12/16).

Despite the abundance of archival instances of refusal to live as a woman and Xie’s unchanging understanding of himself as a man, in Sinophone trans historiography, scholars such as Howard Chiang claim that after a single debrief meeting on the afternoon of August 29th, 1953, where Xie was informed of his doctors’ plans to medically transition him into a woman, “Xie agreed to cooperate in all subsequent medical procedures that would bring about a full sex reassignment” (Chiang 2018, 246). Chiang, as well as Taiwanese scholar Angel Wang (王孝勇, 2020), have proceeded to use feminine pronouns to refer to Xie in their scholarship, as if consent under duress were sufficient to justify the reproduction of medical and archival violence in Sinophone trans historiography, and as if Xie’s own protestations to being medically transitioned throughout the archival traces he left behind were less important than the decision-making of medical authorities that had the ultimate say over Xie’s body and life.

It is impossible to observe Intersex Day of Remembrance in Taiwan without confronting the multiple layers of violence that Xie Jianshun endured, but nevertheless, found ways to defend his dignity as an intersex man throughout the many attempts of doctors, reporters, and institutions to physically and psychologically transform him into a woman he never wanted to become. At the same time, remembrance as resistance is not limited to a single day. As a Taiwanese trans activist organizing against the government’s long-standing insistence on medical authority to validate trans existence as a non-negotiable part of gender recognition, and as an independent scholar attempting to redress the historiographical violences committed by Taiwanese scholars in their telling of Xie’s story, every day is Intersex Day of Remembrance for me. Every day when I nourish my body with feminizing hormones in ways that are deeply gender affirming, I remember the fact that the introduction of estrogen use for gender transition in Taiwan was completely opposite to my experience.

Hormone anniversaries are usually joyous occasions to celebrate one’s gender transition milestones. While I do feel some joy today for myself, what I feel much more intensely is the need for Sinophone trans communities to learn about, remember, and learn from Xie Jianshun’s multiple acts of refusal. Our dignity must be defended, even and especially from those who claim to be in support of transgender liberation while unapologetically writing undignifying histories of Sinophone gender transition. May we remember, on our own terms, what the systems that oppress us have done, and the power that our collective memory can bring to Sinophone transgender movements that refuse compromise, co-optation, and confinement within existing structures of power.

[1] Explanatory note added by 跨服TranServer: The term “sex change” (變性) reflects the original phrasing of 1950s-1960s news and medical archives—language later critiqued for imposing pathologizing.

Chiang, Howard. After Eunuchs Science, Medicine, and the Transformation of Sex in Modern China. Columbia University Press, 2018.

Taiwan shehuixue yanjiu 台灣社會學研究 117(2020): 47-111.

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: 「我的身體為我自己所有」：台灣跨性別與雙性人歷史中的集體記憶、紀念及尊嚴
content:
本篇投稿原刊於跨服TransServer之《跨日典》跨性別共創欄目，在此以《破土雜誌》官網做轉載。在原文中，跨服撰寫了本篇以下的引言：

每年11月是跨性別意識月，11月8日作爲紀念閒性人的日子，承載著跨性別與間性人/雙性人社群所經歷醫療暴力歷史的重量，同時也肩負著在這些社群之間建立團結的責任。有靈選擇這天開始用藥，以此紀念辭作為行動，也賦予其台灣語境的意涵。

醫療體制深刻影響著間性人/雙性人福祉，醫療權威蔓延至個體身體改造之決策，相關學者更進一步透過代筆當事人塑造集體記憶。本文帶著批判與反身性現身，重述謝尖順先生被迫進行性別轉換的檔案及其主體抗爭，向華語跨性別與雙性人社群發出自我尊重的倡議。本文面向廣泛社群的同時，讀者亦須理解學術批判作為獨立疆域的本質，並尊重作者的現身。

11月8日，既是我性別肯認荷爾蒙治療的用藥週年紀念日，又是雙性人紀念日。選擇這個日期開始用藥，有它背後的故事和政治原因。我是一名台灣跨性別倡議者，也是一名從事跨性別研究和台灣戰後跨性別歷史研究的獨立學者。台灣首例使用荷爾蒙進行性別轉換的記載來自於1950年代，且該案例與「性別肯認」相去甚遠。祝願這篇《跨日典》的篇章能提醒我們所有人：守護我們的集體記憶本身就是一種抵抗，尤其是當我們的歷史被一群消費我們的受苦、扭曲並複製醫療與檔案暴力現實，以至損害華語世界跨性別與雙性人集體尊嚴的學者書寫時。

1953年8月14日，台南陸軍第518醫院的醫師們發現，一名名為謝尖順的士兵具有雙性人特徵。醫師們於8月20日進行剖腹探查手術，以確定謝尖順所謂真正的「生理性別」，並判定其解剖結構屬「女性」，因他擁有子宮、兩側卵巢及輸卵管。隨後，醫師們決定，謝尖順該接受「變性」療程，包括後續手術及女性化荷爾蒙治療，以使他成為女性。[1] 期間謝尖順強烈表達了希望繼續以男性身份生活的堅持，甚至在8月21日剖腹探查手術後，向記者表示：「過了卅六個年頭的男子生活，再叫我變成一位女性，那麼我非要自殺不可」（《聯合日報》，1953年8月21日）。關於謝先生性別轉換的檔案資料一貫顯示，他始終將自己視為男性，並對被錯稱為女性以及經醫療介入「被變性」為女性感到極度不適。

1953年稍晚，謝先生接到命令，須從台南的第518醫院轉院至台北的陸海空軍第一總醫院接受進一步「變性」醫療處置，他向記者表示：「我的主張已經決定不上臺北。誰要我去，莫如送我兩粒花生米 (即兩粒子彈的意思)。我寧死不屈。我雖有軍人身分，以服從為天職，但我的身體為我自己所有。我有處理我自己身體之自由」（《民聲日報》，1953年12月9日）。然而，儘管他明確拒絕，仍於1954年初被轉送至台北，繼續接受「治療」。

1955年秋季，第一總醫院的醫師們，為了讓謝先生「能夠做母親」、「便 [他] 的月紅如一般的女性一樣」，並「為了在醫術研究上獲得更偉大的成就」，擅自專購雌激素注射劑給謝先生做實驗（《聯合日報》，1955年10月15日）。關於對注射雌激素的感受，記者訪問謝先生時，報導記載：「針插在體內的痛苦還在其次，眼看自己的身體，一天一天地在起變化， [他] 實在有點躭心」（《聯合日報》，1955年10月17日）。在1950年代台灣軍醫院體系的「照護」下，身為一名士兵，謝先生只能接受當局對其身體所施加的一切，並在那些微小卻充滿力量的時刻，依據他對自身身為男性的認知

author: Brian Hioe
title: The Country That Has Forgotten Joshua Wong
content:
THE SENTENCING of Hong Kong political activist Joshua Wong to an additional ten years in prison, on top of the time that he was already serving, should be a stark warning to Taiwan of the future that it faces if it acquiesces to Chinese political control. Still, one notes that many in Taiwan have forgotten the lessons of Hong Kong.

Wong’s extra ten years in jail were on the basis of alleged collusion with foreign forces. Wong has already spent six years in prison and recently celebrated his 30th birthday behind bars. The new charges mean that by the time Wong gets out of jail, he will be 40. Wong pled guilty to the charges, not because they are true, but as a means to lower his jail sentence.

This proves a tragic fate for Wong, who rose to fame as a youth activist as a teenager. In another future, as one of Hong Kong’s best and brightest, Wong would have taken up leadership in Hong Kong society. Instead, the society that Wong has sacrificed so much for has, because of Chinese political control, locked him away.

Clearly, through locking him away, China aims to hope that the world forgets about his plight, as well as that of many other Hongkongers who are not as internationally well-known as he. Nevertheless, many in Taiwan have already forgotten, or have come to see Hong Kong as a faraway place that offers few lessons for Taiwan.

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Do the US Midterms Mean for Taiwan?
content:
THE US MIDTERM elections resulted in a massive win for Democrats, who made historic gains and took control of both the House and Senate. Consequently, the win has been interpreted as a rebuke to Donald Trump’s presidency.

For its part, the Taiwanese government has sought to reassure that support for Taiwan is bipartisan and that it expects arms sales to continue. Nevertheless, one notes that Trump has himself suspended arms sales, out of an apparent desire to please Chinese president Xi Jinping in trade negotiations.

Analysts have suggested that Trump’s actions may be further constrained after the midterms. After all, Trump is now a lame duck, with two years left in his term. His ability to accomplish his agenda will become further limited with the House and Senate out of his control.

At the same time, Trump may seek to override institutions altogether, tapping into his base. Trump supporters were willing to invade the Capitol as part of an attempted insurrection on January 6, 2021, as part of an attempt to prevent the certification of the 2020 presidential election won by Joe Biden, and they may do so again.

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Does the Taipei Mayoral Debate Tell Us?
content:
THE TAIPEI MAYORAL DEBATE occurred on October 31st, after much discussion ahead of time about whether Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an would be willing to participate. The Shen campaign clamored for a debate, seeing as Shen’s strengths were seen in public speaking and debating, while Chiang is known for sometimes being a stiff public speaker.

The controversy about a police raid on Commander D, a gay bar in Ximending, added to such speculation. Namely, with Chiang stating that he would still attend Pride after the controversy following the raid, the debate was scheduled on the same day as Pride. That Chiang suspended a day of campaigning due to poor health prior to Pride and the debate stoked further speculation. Still, in the end, Chiang appeared at the debate without issue.

Few new policy proposals were made at the debate, which instead was primarily an opportunity for the two candidates to criticize each other and to craft their political images. Shen doubled down on efforts to depict himself as a candidate who is knowledgeable about policy, has a firm grasp of data, and has a vision for Taipei governance. By contrast, Chiang mostly touted the accomplishments of his mayoral administration, and suggested that Shen lacked knowledge of what the Taipei city government was already doing.

Both candidates accused the other of focusing simply on attacks, even as Shen asserted that he has avoided conducting a negative campaign. It is notable that Shen has avoided hyperbolic rhetoric in his campaign to date, even as the overall implication is to suggest that Chiang’s mayoral administration is inept and that he would do better.

On the whole, however, Chiang proved unusually aggressive. Frequent points of criticism alleged that Shen is simply all talk and that his proposals are not rooted in reality, while suggesting that in reality, he does not have the firm grasp of data that he seems to have. Nevertheless, given that Chiang has already accrued an image of not being able to remember facts or produce data off the top of his head, and Shen has built up an image of himself as a nerdy academic, this may not work for Chiang.

To this extent, Chiang’s points of attack on Shen may not be surprising, in appealing to social conservatives. Chiang accused Shen of promoting drug use through his advocacy for harm reduction policies, being weak on crime, and failing to carry out sufficient measures to protect children. This has been a recurring theme for the KMT, in attacking progressive politicians such as Chiang, while calling on them to enact measures to deter crime such as ensuring the continual use of capital punishment. For his part, Shen criticized Chiang for weaponizing the issue at the expense of vulnerable groups such as drug abusers who may need social support to rehabilitate themselves.

Likewise, Chiang attacked Shen on cross-strait policy several times, while also accusing Shen of having orchestrated the Great Recall Movement last year but refusing to admit to it. Shen reaffirmed a stance against mayoral exchanges between Taipei and Shanghai, provided China continues with military threats directed at Taiwan, as well as stating that he would not be against some exchanges such as sports exchanges. At several points, Shen also criticized Chiang for attempting to attack him on issues of national policy, when what is being debated is mayoral policy for Taipei, suggesting that if Chiang was so concerned with national policy, he should return to being a legislator. Shen also attacked Chiang for a poor record in attendance at some government meetings.

On the whole, the debate was what was to be expected, then. Chiang managed a strong enough performance that the debate will probably not impact him as negatively as the Shen campaign would have hoped, which is probably why the Shen campaign has called for further debates to take place, with the view that Chiang might slip up in a future debate in such a fashion as to give the Shen campaign political ammunition that could be used against him. It is unclear whether this debate will take place, with the Chiang campaign remaining reluctant to debate.

At the same time, Chiang was clearly on the defensive, which is what pushed him to a combative attitude against Shen. It is, of course, Shen whose banners are visible throughout Taipei streets, and who commands a substantial share of media attention, such that it is his mayoral campaign that has breathed new life into DPP campaigns across Taiwan. Chiang was hoping to run a conservative campaign where he said as little as possible and touted existing accomplishments in Taipei, which is considered politically safe for the KMT, but the rise of Puma Shen as a tough challenger with a seemingly bold and new vision for Taipei has instead put him on the defensive, and at this late stage in the game, it is too late for Chiang to reinvent his image or pledge to have some competing vision for Taipei in his second term.

author: Dinah Gardner
title: The Other China We Need to Talk About
content:
WHAT IF I told you that there was a chance—not a very high chance, but a real chance nonetheless—that if you visited the People’s Republic of China today you might be kidnapped, blindfolded, driven to a specialized facility and subjected to six months of psychological torture. All on the orders of the state.

It sounds unbelievable, doesn’t it?

But this is what happened to at least several dozen foreign citizens in recent years. It is what happened to American scholar Min Zin this past June, when he landed in Yunnan province on the invitation of a Chinese academic institution to attend a conference. And it is also what happened to half a dozen people who appear in the latest edition of the book The People’s Republic of the Disappeared, which we just published on 28 October.

This important book is a collection of mostly first-person stories that expose the psychological horrors of being held in the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) feared secret detention system called Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL). The system permits police to hold an individual in complete isolation, no contact with family or lawyers, to be interrogated for hours at will.

The individual is under 24-hour guard: this includes being watched all day every day, all night every night, whether you are asleep, sitting quietly in your cell or even on the toilet. The CCP intentionally uses RSDL to strip away every last shred of human dignity. RSDL is designed to break a person’s will to extract a confession for crimes imagined by the state

For more than a decade, the CCP has used RSDL against its own people, in particular human rights defenders. It is now increasingly using it against foreign citizens to exert its will across borders and as a kind of hostage diplomacy. Michael Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who wrote the foreword to this edition, is one of its most well-known examples.

In editing the stories for this book, I was struck again and again by how similar everyone’s experience was. This speaks to the uniformity of the RSDL system:

The removal of the temporal world. “There are no clocks in RSDL” is the title of Australian TV anchor Cheng Lei’s chapter. She would guess and count breaths to keep track of time.

The removal of the physical world. There are no windows in RSDL or they are covered in thick blackout curtains. Japanese scholar Hideji Suzuki cried when he was granted 15 minutes of sunlight, the only time in his seven months’ incarceration when he was allowed to see the sky.

The removal of yourself. Michael Kovrig noted: “There are no mirrors—not even the reassurance of seeing your own face.” Chinese activist Li Qiaochu writes how she was simply called “target”.

Filling the space left by these absences was a current of fear. Endless rules, the lack of privacy yet total isolation (guards were forbidden from talking to prisoners), reduced nutrition, sleep deprivation, lack of fresh air, and the padded suicide-proofed walls. Several of the detainees wrote while they could never see outside their RSDL facility, at nighttime they would often hear gunfire or the barking of dogs.

“In my mentally exhausted state, the sounds of gunfire would constantly startle me and even cause me to imagine that I was about to be executed,” wrote Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che.

But something else struck me as I read through their testimonies. However harrowing these stories of suffering are, they are also evidence of human resilience in the face of horror.

Cheng Lei writes about how she would escape into her mind, translating poems, reliving her former TV interviews and making up stories in her head. Similarly, Michael Kovrig meditated, sang songs to himself, and remembered past moments in his life, as if it was a recording playing in his mind.

“I learned to meditate on the movies I had watched and the poems and novels I had read,” wrote Li Qiaochu. “Those precious memories allowed me to gradually filter out the brainwashing, to preserve my vitality and to keep myself from being transformed into their machine.”

Feedback from earlier editions informed us that rights activists use the Chinese editions of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared to prepare for and strengthen their mental resolve and courage in case one day they too are taken into RSDL. Knowing that others have gone through this and come out the other side can be an immense help. It’s for this reason that the Chinese edition of this book will be available free to download as a PDF from our website.

In a world where influencers and media wax lyrical about the futuristic cities, advanced technologies and amazing sights in China, in a world where it’s a desirable goal to be Chinamaxxing, we need to remember that there is another side to China, a much darker side.

That is why we are publishing this third edition of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared in English, focusing this time on foreign citizens as targets. Foreigners who never imagined they would be kidnapped by the CCP.

We cannot let the world forget that this is how the world’s second superpower behaves or we will all lose our human dignity in the end.

The English version of the book is available in multiple formats from Amazon. All money raised goes into our urgent actions and advocacy work.

title: Endangered Eastern Grass Owl Habitat Threatened by Shalun Science Park
content:
ENVIRONMENTALISTS HAVE warned of the potential displacement of the Eastern grass owl as a result of the construction of the Shalun Science Park.

The Eastern grass owl is a critically endangered species in Taiwan, with its habitat including Tainan, Chiayi, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung, and it is Taiwan’s only owl species that nests in grasslands. After much effort by environmentalists to rebuild its habitat on the Dadu Mountain Plateau, the Eastern grass owl was found to have returned to central Taiwan earlier this year. It is thought that the Eastern grass owl disappeared from central Taiwan in the 1960s.

Environmentalists voiced concerns about the owl’s habitat at the second-stage environmental impact review, whose scoping session concluded on October 12th. The planned development zones “Parking 1” and “Industrial 1-2” would threaten the habitat of the Eastern grass owl, in that the current area is considered top-tier nesting grounds for the owl. As such, developers were urged to create habitats for the Eastern grass owl before construction. The Kaohsiung Science Park has been cited as an example of where development has already displaced the Eastern grass owl.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Pakistan Abruptly Cancels Taiwanese Overflight Routes Then Reverses Course
content:
IN AN UNUSUAL series of events, in short order, Pakistan declared that Taiwanese airlines would not be allowed to fly over the country, then reversed course on the decision.

The decision was announced by Pakistan’s Minister of Defense Khawaja Asif, who stated that the new policy was made to comply with Pakistan’s One China Policy. Originally, Taiwanese airlines EVA Air and China Airlines had been cleared for overflight privileges by Pakistan from October 28 of this year through March 27, 2027, as approved by the country’s Civil Aviation Authority.

This would be the first time that a country has revoked overflight privileges for Taiwanese air carriers, on the basis of a claimed One China Policy. If so, it could be that Pakistan would be seeking closer ties with China, and hitting out at Taiwan would be a means of doing so. Or Pakistan could have been acting on China’s behest, with China expected to try and constrain Taiwan’s international space ahead of the upcoming local elections next month. As for why Pakistan later reversed course, this is also unclear, except perhaps that international backlash was larger than expected–or perhaps there was pressure behind the scenes from the US.

author: Brian Hioe
title: China Steps Up Transnational Repression Ahead of Elections
content:
CHINA HAS STEPPED up efforts to intimidate Taiwan ahead of elections in November. This has occurred with the usual combination of domestic threats and military exercises. Nevertheless, one can point to a discernible effort to project power over Taiwan.

In particular, China released high-resolution satellite images of Taiwan, as well as a propaganda poster, on the anniversary of the handover of Taiwan from Japanese to ROC control.

The satellite imagery was designed to convey a sense of having already penetrated Taiwan, such that it can observe Taiwan easily from without–and to contribute to the sense that the Chinese military could take Taiwan at any time. To this extent, as with any display of Chinese military hardware, this would also be signalling between the two militaries, with the Chinese government showing its capacities to the ROC military as a means of intimidation.

One can perceive attacks that have occurred in Taiwan in recent memory as similarly aimed at projecting power. News broke earlier this month of the indictment of five men over a plot to hit stand-up comic Huang Yi-hao with a car, in retribution for a comedy show in which Huang mocked Chinese president Xi Jinping.

title: What Explains the Rise of Puma Shen as a DPP Candidate in Taipei?
content:
THE METEORIC RISE of Puma Shen as the DPP’s Taipei mayoral candidate has made what was previously perceived as a relatively slow election into an unpredictable and exciting one. It is generally expected that Shen, whether or not he wins the Taipei mayorship, could be the best-performing DPP Taipei mayoral candidate since Chen Shui-bian in 1992–Chen, of course, later became president.

Shen being sent to run in Taipei was originally perceived as his being sent there as a sacrificial candidate. After all, Shen was previously mainly known for tough stances on China, as the founder of the Doublethink Lab, which researches Chinese disinformation, and of the Kuma Academy, Taiwan’s best-known civil defense organization. It would be expected that he would struggle in historically pan-Blue Taipei. Running Shen, then, would be to field a younger and untested candidate for Taipei, whereas running another post-Sunflower politician, such as Enoch Wu, who had previously contested Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an unsuccessfully, would have been seen as putting little effort into the race. Shen, as a party list legislator, had never had to run an electoral campaign before.

author: Ming-Yeh T. Rawnsley
title: Women and Taiwan’s Next Economic Transformation
content:
IN 2015, ECONOMIST Elliott Fan (樊家忠) encountered a result that his collaborators found difficult to believe. An experiment involving 450 residents of Taipei and New Taipei City showed no statistically significant difference between men’s and women’s willingness to compete. Studies elsewhere had frequently found men more inclined to enter competitive situations. In his Taiwanese sample, that familiar gap was absent.

Fan checked the procedures and sample but found no mistake that explained the result. The finding prompted a larger inquiry: what had shaped women’s opportunities and expectations in Taiwan?

Women’s participation in work, business and politics helped shape Taiwan’s transformation even as economic change opened new possibilities for them. That relationship matters again as the semiconductor economy enters the AI boom. Access to technology careers will influence who shares in its rewards and who helps direct its development.

In a podcast interview released in October by the NTNU International Taiwan Studies Center, in collaboration with the International Journal of Taiwan Studies, the National Taiwan University professor explored how agriculture, business, migration and electoral politics had changed women’s lives. His research suggests that gender expectations respond to economic opportunities and institutional rules. The same attention to those conditions is needed as technology reshapes careers.

TAIWAN, JAPAN, AND SOUTH KOREA share aspects of a Confucian heritage, including traditions assigning women responsibility for care. Yet their gender outcomes differ. Fan points to women’s visibility in Taiwanese politics and business as reasons to question explanations that treat culture as a fixed constraint. His experimental finding invites scrutiny of the circumstances in which gender differences emerge.

One explanation begins in colonial Taiwan. Sugar production expanded under Japanese rule, requiring substantially more labor than rice cultivation. Women became more deeply involved in agricultural production, increasing their contribution to household income.

Women’s contribution to household income could strengthen their bargaining position within the family. Yet they continued to cook, clean and care for children while taking on more fieldwork. Greater economic importance came with a heavier workload. That tension remains relevant to technology careers, where access to paid work may expand without a corresponding redistribution of unpaid care.

Nevertheless, demand for women’s labor could unsettle established restrictions. In research published in 2022 with Nora Cheng and economic historian Wu Tsong-min, Fan links expanding sugar-cane cultivation to the abandonment of foot-binding in early twentieth-century Taiwan. In the NTNU podcast, he also describes higher postwar female labor-force participation in former sugar-growing areas than in rice-growing areas, suggesting that changes in women’s productive roles could influence later generations.

These consequences do not make colonial exploitation a project of emancipation. They show how economic demands could alter household relations, with effects extending beyond the intentions of those directing development.

FAN’S SECOND EXPLANATION concerns Taiwan’s small and medium-sized enterprises. In a small firm, an owner may know employees’ capabilities directly. A capable woman may gain responsibility without passing through numerous layers of management dominated by men.

Family succession creates another route: daughters may take over when there is no son, when a son does not wish to continue the business, or when a daughter is better placed to lead. Across an economy with many family businesses, these decisions can create substantial opportunities for women to exercise authority.

Fan’s work on firm size and gender equity remains in progress, and small firms are not automatically fair. The important question is how business structures affect access to leadership. Applied to technology careers, this means examining how people are recruited, recognized and promoted, alongside encouraging women to gain technical qualifications.

His third inquiry concerns postwar migration. Military dependents’ villages, known as juancun (眷村), brought mainland Chinese migrants into contact with surrounding Taiwanese communities. Fan describes comparisons associating proximity to these settlements with greater female labor-force participation, later marriage and weaker son preference among local Taiwanese residents.

This research also remains in progress. Fan suggests that everyday contact transmitted different expectations about women and family life, without implying uniform attitudes within either population. Gender norms may change through encounters between neighbors as well as through changes in the workplace.

POLITICAL REPRESENTATION offers a more direct example of institutional design. Taiwan’s local electoral quotas reserve seats for women according to the number of seats in a district. Fan and his co-authors use variation generated by these rules to examine the effects of exposure to female political leadership.

Their findings, published in the Journal of Development Economics in 2025, extend beyond elections. They found evidence of weaker son preference, greater participation by married women in household decisions, and increased interest among female students in studying law and political science.

The results are consistent with a role-model effect. Seeing women exercise public authority can expand other women’s sense of what is possible. For a student choosing a university subject, political leadership becomes a career she can imagine pursuing.

This suggests a question for technology employers and educators: who is visible as an expert or leader, and whose ambitions receive support? The political findings do not establish that identical interventions will work in technology. They do show that institutional changes can influence career aspirations beyond the people who benefit directly.

FAN WORRIES that the expansion of a male-dominated AI industry could concentrate access to highly paid jobs among men, making further progress toward wage equality harder. His warning concerns who captures the gains from growth; it does not establish that AI has already reversed Taiwan’s progress.

The historical lesson is that participation depends on how opportunities are organized. Encouraging girls to study science and technology is part of the task. Access also depends on recruitment, promotion and working arrangements that allow people with caring responsibilities to build careers. Women need opportunities to acquire authority and shape decisions as well as enter the workforce.

Following Fan’s argument means asking practical questions. Can women enter technical fields through retraining as well as university education? Are promotion criteria transparent? Can workers take parental leave without losing access to career-building assignments? These are ways to examine whether the promise of opportunity reaches beyond recruitment campaigns.

Technology careers could reproduce the uneven bargain of the sugar fields if access expands without changes to the organization of work and care.

Asked which university major will offer the best prospects in the AI age, Fan answers: ‘I don’t know, because nobody knows’. Uncertainty about future jobs need not prevent action on the barriers that already restrict people’s choices.

Taiwan’s next economic transformation will be shaped by decisions about education, employment and authority as well as technological advances. Its success should be judged partly by whether women gain secure careers, share in the rewards and help decide how new technologies are used. Women helped build the economy that made this transformation possible. They should have a full part in shaping what comes next.

title: Labor Groups Seek to Put Demands on Agenda Ahead of Election
content:

A strike by workers at iconic snack Kuai Kuai’s Zhongli factory came to an end after five days earlier this month. author: Brian Hioe
title: Political Parties Spar Over Taiwan’s Demographic Woes
content:
THE KMT HAS hit out at the DPP’s failure to correct Taiwan’s demographic woes, crticizing the decline in the national population. According to the National Development Council, Taiwan’s population is expected to fall below 20 million by 2045. Taiwan’s population is expected to halve by 2075.

Specifically, the KMT has made a new savings plan it proposed that the DPP rejected, the Taiwan Youth Development and Future Account Act, as proof that the DPP does not care about the issue. The act would have allocated an “Education and Development Account” and “Taiwan Future Account” to each child, the former of which would be able to be used at any time, and the latter of which would be accessible at age 18. 60,000 NT would be provided to each child per year under the proposal. The KMT has also hit out at the inability of the government to construct more social housing.

Nevertheless, one notes that the DPP rejected the Taiwan Youth Development and Future Account Act on the basis that it, in allowing for corporate sponsors, it could increase the gaps in inequality. The DPP has instead proposed a similar proposal that would also allow for 60,000 NT to be allocated to each child annually.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Car Crash Plot on Comedian Shows Increasing Violence of China’s Transnational Repression
content:
FIVE MEN WERE indicted earlier this week over a plot to run down stand-up comic Huang Yi-hao, in retribution for a comedy show in which Huang mocked Chinese president Xi Jinping.

The five men slammed into Huang with a car, injuring his pelvis, after being ordered to hurt Huang enough to hospitalize him. Subsequently, they acted as though the incident was an accident and assisted Huang with an insurance claim. They then forwarded the picture of the insurance documentation to their handler, a Chinese man referred to in media reporting as K., who refused to pay them the full 450,000 NT promised because Huang was not injured sufficiently.

News of the plot to attack Huang follows suit from the indictment of two men over a May attack on a comedy club where Huang was performing, during which the comedy club had a mixture of feces and paint thrown at its entrance. A 35-year-old man surnamed Kuo was reportedly paid 50,000 NT by a 33-year-old man surnamed Liu to carry out the attack. It is unclear whether the two were acting at China’s behest. The incident was not widely known before the indictment.

Since news of the plot broke, there have been calls to strengthen national security laws to deal with Chinese threats. In particular, the attack on the comedy club and the plot to run down Huang highlight China’s growing transnational repression within Taiwan itself.

author: Brian Hioe
title: KMT Passes National Health Insurance Policy To Benefit Seniors, At Risk Of Fiscal Sustainability
content:
MINISTER OF HEALTH and Welfare Shih Chung-liang has criticized new legislation that would require the government to fully cover National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums for people aged 65 and older whose total consolidated income has an income tax rate of less than 20 percent. Such individuals would no longer have to pay premiums. Specifically, Shih has criticized the proposal as putting the burden for the NHI on working-age taxpayers, seeing as medical services are used disproportionately by the young and elderly, when Taiwan already has among the world’s lowest health insurance premiums.

The proposal has been criticized in the past as favoring elderly taxpayers and exempting them from having to pay health insurance premiums. In this way, apart from putting the burden of covering NHI premiums on working-age people, it has been criticized as benefiting wealthy elderly individuals.

Those who pay 20% in income tax are those who make above 1,330,000 NT per year. Those who make below 590,000 NT per year pay a 5% income tax premium. The KMT later amended the idea to only exempt seniors who pay under 5% in income tax. But the Ministry of Health and Welfare then warned that the proposal would lead to a loss of 54 billion NT for the NHI each year.

Taiwan’s universal health insurance system enjoys bipartisan support. Nevertheless, the KMT would be aiming to please a core support demo

author: Brian Hioe
title: Despite Budget Passage, Defense Items Remain Frozen on Legislative Agenda
content:
QUESTIONS ABOUT defense procurement have been raised, with less than two months in the fiscal year, and the legislature’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee not having scheduled any review of over 150 requests to unfreeze funding.

The KMT finally relented on budgetary spending–including defense spending–in August, this being more than 351 days after the budget was submitted by the Executive Yuan for review. Though defense spending was passed, this was in the form of part of the Executive Yuan’s regular budget, rather than as a special operational expense.

The conditions of passage also froze funds or subject them to yearly approval by the legislature. Among what was cut was 10% of funding for the Taiwan Tactical Mission Network and the Team Awareness Kit, while the KMT also slashed additional funding for programs it does not like, such as funding for Taiwan’s domestic submarine fleet after the initial submarine, the Hai Kun. That drone funding is subject to additional approval by the legislature makes it difficult for industry to have assurances of continued funding if this is subject to change every year. Apart from the Taiwan Tactical Mission Network and the Team Awareness Kit, which provide for situational awareness, the military has also submitted requests to unfreeze maintenance and replenishment parts for its M1A2T Abrams tanks.

author: Girard Mariano Lopez
title: Taipei Grand Mosque Board Faces Eviction Threat, Sparking Protests
content:
A DISPUTE OVER control of the Taipei Grand Mosque has spilled into protest after court enforcement against its board’s bank funds—raising concerns about donations, charitable services, and management of the historic religious site.

Dozens of Muslims from more than 10 countries gathered outside the Chinese Muslim Association’s office on October 16th. Organizers said demonstrations would continue every Friday after prayers until association leaders publicly addressed their concerns.

Yaser Cheng, chairman of the Taipei Grand Mosque Foundation, said the dispute threatened resources supporting a congregation that includes migrant workers and international students.

“They took the money from us,” Cheng said in an interview, describing funds he said included small donations from Indonesian workers and other worshippers. “It’s not from our board pocket.”

The Chinese Muslim Association, or CMA, has yet to respond to requests for an interview.

The conflict centers on competing claims over property rights and the authority to manage the mosque, which opened in 1960 and became a Taipei municipal historic monument in 1999. It remains a place of worship and a gathering point for Taiwan’s international Muslim community.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Chinese Student Deported Over Online Video
content:
A CHINESE STUDENT studying in Taiwan has been deported over a video showing him pinching Lai Ching-te. The post on Douyin, in particular, occurred after the student in question attended an event that Lai Ching-te spoke at on Monday at National Taiwan University and posted a video showing him pinching Lai in his fingers.

The student posted “Lai Ching-te is right in front of you. Could this be the only chance in your lifetime?”, along with the hashtags “#Cross-strait unification,” “#Oppose Taiwan independence,” and “#May Taiwan soon return to the motherland.”

The student later deleted the post and apologized, but the National Immigration Agency (NIA) had already decided to revoke his residency in Taiwan and deport him. The NIA claimed that the student had violated Article 12 of the Regulations Governing Permission for People of the Mainland Area to Enter the Taiwan Area, which states that “conduct that violates the principles of equality and dignity” is sufficient grounds for deportation.

Not all members of the Lai administration have supported the deportation. Shortly before the deportation was announced, Straits Exchange Foundation secretary-general Luo Wen-jia stated that he supported the student being allowed to complete his studies in Taiwan, if he so wished. Afterward, Luo stated that he supported the decision of relevant authorities.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Animal Rights Advocates Call for Referendum on Snare Traps
content:
ANIMAL RIGHTS ADVOCATES are currently campaigning for a referendum to be held on the use of wild boar snares.

In particular, animal rights advocates have long criticized wild boar snares as overly cruel. Such traps use spring-loaded mechanisms to tighten around animals’ limbs when triggered.

Nevertheless, such traps have also been criticized for ensnaring other species, as they do not distinguish. Endangered species such as Formosan black bears and leopard cats had also been killed by such traps, as have cats and dogs, sometimes resulting in their losing limbs if they survive.

Though claims had been made that Indigenous hunters used such traps as part of traditional hunting rights, animal rights groups have generally cited that this was rarely the case, in that Indigenous hunters generally do not use such traps. By contrast, such animal rights advocates state that Indigenous hunters more commonly use traps made from wood, bamboo and vines, and other natural materials. In the past, the Central Election Commission turned down calls for a referendum on the use of wild boar snares on the basis that the referendum was unclear as to whether it pertained to traps used by Indigenous hunters.

author: Brian Hioe
title: In A First, China Sanctions Ministers of Diplomatic Allies of Taiwan
content:
THE CHINESE GOVERNMENT has sanctioned two government ministers from diplomatic allies of Taiwan. These would be Belizean Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca and Paraguayan Minister of Information Gustavo Villate. Such sanctions prevent them and their family members from doing business in China.

China does not appear to have sanctioned ministers of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies in the past. This would be a new means, then, of pressuring countries to switch ties from Taiwan to China.

Taiwan is larger than all of its diplomatic allies, whether measured in terms of the size of population or economy. The main reason why Taiwan maintains ties with its diplomatic allies is so that they can speak up for it in international organizations in which Taiwan is not a member.

That being said, Taiwan has also long been accused of “dollar diplomacy”–paying off diplomatic allies through infrastructure investment deals or slush money to high-ranking politicians in return for recognition. Indeed, one notes that many of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies are countries that have questionable human rights records.

Though China offers much the same to such allies in return for switching recognition, Taiwan is unable to outspend China. China is, of course, much larger than Taiwan. Likewise, small states risk being shut ouf of the lucrative–and much larger–Chinese market if they retain ties with Taiwan.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Army Suicide Reminds of Recurring Issues with Bullying and Hazing in the Military
content:
A RECENT CASE in which a female Army first lieutenant committed suicide is being investigated as a potential case of bullying. The first lieutenant in question, surnamed Wang, jumped to her death from a building at the Army’s 206th Brigade base in Hsinchu County on September 30th. An audio recording that was posted on Threads on October 12th shows a man berating Wang for failing to heed instructions, leading to the bullying allegations.

The Ministry of National Defense has vowed that the case is being investigated and that Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo is attentive to its developments. This would not be the only case in recent years in which a suicide in the military has been linked to bullying.

In November 2020, a similar case emerged of a corporal surnamed Liu stationed in the Eighth Army Command’s 203rd Brigade in Danei District, Tainan, who died by hanging. Liu, too, was reportedly bullied by his superiors and peers.

The most famous case of a death in the military thought to have resulted from bullying in the military would be the death of cadet Hung Chung-chiu in July 2013. Hung is thought to have been bullied by his superiors and peers shortly before his discharge from mandatory military service, as a form of hazing or as retribution against him before his service ended. author: Brian Hioe
title: Delivery Workers Criticize Plans by Grab to Acquire Foodpanda
content:
DELIVERY WORKERS from the National Delivery Workers’ Union demonstrated outside the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) earlier this month against plans by Grab to acquire Foodpanda. Specifically, delivery workers have criticized that the acquisition of Foodpanda by Grab would create monopoly conditions that would be detrimental to workers’ rights.

Taiwan’s food delivery landscape is already a duopoly between Foodpanda and Uber. Uber holds 13% of shares in Grab. Likewise, previously Uber sought to acquire Foodpanda in a deal that was blocked by the Fair Trade Commission. As such, Uber is accused of potentially seeking to acquire Foodpanda through a different means.

At the time, the National Food Delivery Workers’ Union called for the FTC to investigate the impact of the deal on workers’ and consumers’ rights, as well as the impact of what a monopoly would be. Namely, Uber Eats and Foodpanda were already criticized in the past as unilaterally raising costs for workers and prices for consumers, and the former’s acquisition of the latter may make this problem more severe.

Nevertheless, one notes that Grab has also been criticized over potential links to China. Consequently, members of the National Delivery Workers’ Union were joined by the Economic Democracy Union and DPP politicians such as Wang Shih-chien and Kao Chia-yu. Grab was singled out for past cooperation with Huawei on mappi

author: Brian Hioe
title: Taiwan Again Rolls Out the Red Carpet for an Authoritarian Monarch For National Day
content:
KING MSWATI III of Eswatini was recently in Taiwan for National Day. As a result, the red carpet was once again rolled out for the authoritarian monarch, who presides over Africa’s last absolute monarchy, by the Lai administration.

In particular, apart from Mswati III’s presence at National Day, President Lai Ching-te and Mswati III visited Taiwan’s Air Force Command. Lai touted support from Mswati III on establishing the Taiwan Industrial Innovation Park, as well as Eswatini’s role as Taiwan’s gateway into Africa. Eswatini is Taiwan’s only remaining diplomatic ally in Africa.

Ties between Eswatini and the Lai administration have been in the spotlight in recent years, especially after a dramatic visit to the country by Lai. In May, a planned trip by the Taiwanese president for King Mswati III’s 58th birthday and the 40th anniversary of his accession to the throne was abruptly canceled.

This occurred because countries that Lai would have passed over on his flight to Eswatini, Madagascar, Mauritius, and the Seychelles revoked overflight permissions shortly before Lai was to set out. This was largely interpreted as China flexing its muscles in terms of its influence in Africa, with the Lai administration suggesting that China threatened to revoke debt cancellation for Madagascar, Mauritius, and the Seychelles if they did not comply.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Why Would Chiang Wan-an Propose Replacing Songshan Airport with an “AI Park”?
content:
IN AN UNUSUAL proposal, Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an has proposed replacing Songshan Airport with an AI park. Chiang claims that this AI park would involve not only technological facilities, but also greenery and residential areas.

This is not the first time such a proposal has been made. In the past, DPP political candidates such as Lee Ying-yuan in 2002, Frank Hsieh in 2006, and Enoch Wu in 2022 have made similar proposals to move Songshan Airport and to replace it with a park.

Nevertheless, the central government has rejected such proposals in the past, citing security concerns. High-level officials usually travel from Taiwan to other countries through Songshan Airport, as do foreign dignitaries. Songshan Airport also serves some functions for the Taiwanese military, as it is guarded by it because of the view that the Chinese military would seek to capture it in the event of an invasion. Located in downtown Taipei, Songshan Airport is the smaller airport that serves Taipei besides Taoyuan International Airport. Unlike Taoyuan International Airport, it is located inside the city rather than outside of it.

Flights to Taiwan’s outlying islands are usually serviced outside of Songshan Airport. In recent years, short-range flights to Japan and South Korea have also operated from Songshan Airport. Indeed, it is hard to imagine that residents of Taiwan’s outlying islands would be
